query: For CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys (X = Si, Mn, or Al) in a single- or multiphase metallic solid-solution state, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain whether a stable, coherent protective oxide layer forms and persists during exposure above 900 °C in an oxidative or corrosive atmosphere, rather than developing unstable surface oxides that crack or spall? Specify what governs the behaviour and why, a controlled comparison against a defined baseline, the predicted differences, the applicable exposure and material-state boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a falsifying observation.

generation.hypothesis: In CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys, the formation and persistence of a stable, coherent oxide scale at temperatures above 900 °C is mainly governed by the nature of the reactive element X. Specifically, when X is Al, a protective and adherent Al2O3 scale forms due to its low growth kinetics and high thermodynamic stability, whereas when X is Mn (or similarly less effective elements), the alloy develops unstable manganese oxides that are prone to cracking and spallation.
generation.material_initial_state: CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys in a single- or multiphase metallic solid-solution state, where X is varied among Si, Mn, or Al.
generation.intervention: Replace the reactive element X in the alloy with Al (i.e., produce a CrFeCoNiAl alloy) and compare its oxidation behavior against a baseline alloy containing Mn as X.
generation.conditions: Expose both alloys to an oxidative or corrosive atmosphere at temperatures above 900 °C using identical oxidation testing protocols (e.g., isothermal oxidation for a fixed duration under controlled gas composition).
generation.structural_mediator: The coherence and integrity of the surface oxide scale, specifically the formation of a continuous, adherent Al2O3 layer versus non-coherent, unstable manganese oxide layers.
generation.mechanism: Aluminum’s strong affinity for oxygen and its tendency to form a slow-growing, thermodynamically stable Al2O3 layer results in a coherent and effective diffusion barrier against further oxidation. In contrast, manganese has a higher diffusivity and can lead to rapid formation of non-protective, cracked manganese oxides, which spall from the surface under high-temperature conditions.
generation.predicted_outcome: The alloy with X = Al will display a lower overall oxidation rate, maintain a uniform and adherent oxide layer (primarily Al2O3), and resist spallation under extended exposure above 900 °C, whereas the baseline Mn-containing alloy will develop unstable, cracked oxide scales.
generation.boundary: Tested at temperatures above 900 °C in an oxidative or corrosive atmosphere, while maintaining the initial single- or multiphase metallic solid-solution state of the high-entropy alloy.
generation.uncertainty: While the qualitative protective effect of Al is supported by thermodynamic and diffusional considerations, the exact quantitative differences in oxidation kinetics and scale thickness between the alloys may vary with processing history, exact compositional ratios, and microstructural details.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize two sets of CrFeCoNiX high-entropy alloys using identical processing routes—one set with X = Al and the other with X = Mn. Expose samples from both sets to an oxidative or corrosive environment at temperatures above 900 °C for a fixed time period under identical conditions.
measurements: X-ray diffraction (XRD) to identify the oxide phases and assess their crystallinity
Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) on cross sections to evaluate oxide layer coherence, thickness, and spallation
Mass gain measurements (e.g., thermogravimetric analysis) to compare oxidation kinetics
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Al-containing alloy does not exhibit a significantly more coherent, stable, and slower-growing oxide scale compared to the Mn-containing alloy under identical test conditions, or if the expected protective Al2O3 phase is not predominant, then the hypothesis would be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Cr’s outward diffusion is faster than oxygen’s inward diffusion, so chromia scales usually grow outward, consisting of fractions of iron, nickel, and manganese. However, at temperatures above 900 °C, chromia can form volatile CrO3. Aluminum, another effective alloying element, forms a protective Al2O3 layer, offering significant resistance to high-temperature oxidation and corrosion. Al2O3 scales grow slower than chromium oxide scales and are more stable, especially against aggressive carbon or sulfur species. However, the formation of alumina and consequent depletion of Al in the alloy could result in structural instability in the alloy. The formation of oxide scales in HEAs containing multiple oxide-forming species is influenced by their intricate chemistries and microstructures. High-temperature, long-duration oxidation studies on bulk alloys typically reveal dominant oxide films composed of complex ternary and quaternary oxides. The polycrystalline nature of these alloys, combined with surface heterogeneity and phase instabilities at high temperatures, leads to highly variable oxide structures. cited_evidence.text: In the case of the Mn15Al5 alloy, the outer part of the oxide layer was mainly composed of Mn, suggesting the presence of MnxOy oxides followed by a thin layer of Cr-based oxides found at the metal/oxide interface. Moreover, a significant level of porosity was found within its closest proximity of it. The overall thickness of the whole layer after 100 h annealing reached approximately 25 µm. More importantly, the Mn15Al5 alloy was the only one showing strong sub-surface oxidation and developed internal porosity due to the diffusion of Mn toward the oxide layer. It was found that the sub-surface porosity reached up to ≈100 µm into the alloy core and likely may further progress with the increasing time of annealing. The present oxides within the metal were mainly composed of Mn and Al. Increasing the content of Al above 5 at.% resulted in a completely different behavior, forming a well-protective oxide layer containing foremostly Al, suggesting the formation of AlxOy without any traces of chipping or formation of sub-surface oxides.
